UKPDS (1998) showed that intensive glucose control reduced microvascular complications, with long-term follow-up revealing a legacy benefit, and metformin appeared to reduce cardiovascular events in overweight patients. However, ACCORD (2008) found increased mortality when HbA1c was driven very low, showing that the route to a lower HbA1c matters as much as the number.

In 2008 US regulators began requiring cardiovascular safety trials for new glucose-lowering drugs. These trials changed practice. EMPA-REG OUTCOME (2015) showed that the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death in patients with established cardiovascular disease, and LEADER (2016) showed that the GLP-1 receptor agonist liraglutide reduced major cardiovascular events. SGLT2 inhibitors were then found to reduce heart failure hospitalisation and progression of chronic kidney disease, for example in CREDENCE (2019) and DAPA-CKD (2020). These benefits appear only partly explained by glucose lowering.

NICE NG28 reflects this shift. Since its February 2026 update it recommends offering an SGLT2 inhibitor alongside metformin as initial therapy for most adults with type 2 diabetes, rather than reserving it for those with heart failure, cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease, and adds the GLP-1 receptor agonist semaglutide from the start for people with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Weight has also become a treatment target: GLP-1 based therapies produce substantial weight loss, and DiRECT (2018) showed that intensive weight management can induce remission.

Yet glucose has not become irrelevant. Hyperglycaemia still drives retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy, symptoms and infections, and NICE still sets individualised HbA1c targets while avoiding hypoglycaemia, particularly in frail older people. Comprehensive risk management, including blood pressure, statins and smoking cessation, contributes much of the cardiovascular benefit. Newer drugs are costly, have adverse effects such as genital infection, euglycaemic DKA and gastrointestinal intolerance, and supply problems and unequal access persist.

The claim is therefore largely right: drug choice is now driven by heart, kidney and weight outcomes. A better description is that glucose control has been placed within organ protection rather than replaced by it.

questions.q: Mrs Lewis, 68, is admitted confused and dehydrated. She has lost weight and has back pain. Measured calcium 2.85 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L, PTH suppressed, creatinine 145 µmol/L (baseline 80), haemoglobin 98 g/L, ESR 95 mm/h. She takes no thiazides or supplements. (a) Calculate adjusted calcium. (b) Give a differential diagnosis and the most likely cause. (c) Outline investigations and acute management.
markScheme: Suppressed PTH indicates PTH-independent hypercalcaemia, excluding primary hyperparathyroidism
Differential: malignancy (bone metastases, PTHrP, myeloma), vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease, thiazides, immobilisation
Anaemia, renal impairment, bone pain and high ESR suggest multiple myeloma
Investigations: serum protein electrophoresis, serum free light chains, urine Bence Jones protein, imaging of skeleton (whole-body low-dose CT or MRI)
Also check PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, phosphate, ALP, and search for solid tumour if myeloma negative
IV 0.9% sodium chloride rehydration with fluid balance monitoring
IV bisphosphonate after rehydration, adjusted for renal function; denosumab if renal function precludes bisphosphonate
Stop calcium-raising drugs (thiazides, calcium and vitamin D supplements); monitor ECG and electrolytes
Glucocorticoids may help myeloma and granulomatous causes; haematology referral for definitive treatment
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Adjusted calcium = 2.85 + 0.02 × (40 − 34) = 2.85 + 0.12 = 2.97 mmol/L, just below the 3.0 mmol/L level usually used to define moderate hypercalcaemia, but clearly symptomatic, explaining her confusion and dehydration.

(b) A suppressed PTH shows the parathyroids are responding appropriately, so primary hyperparathyroidism is excluded. PTH-independent causes include malignancy (by PTHrP from squamous, renal or breast tumours, osteolytic metastases, or myeloma), vitamin D excess, granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis with extra-renal calcitriol production, thiazides, milk-alkali syndrome and immobilisation. The combination of back pain, normocytic anaemia, acute kidney injury and a very high ESR in an older woman makes multiple myeloma the most likely diagnosis.

(c) Investigations include serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains and urinary Bence Jones protein. Skeletal imaging, now usually whole-body low-dose CT or MRI rather than a plain skeletal survey, looks for lytic lesions. A blood film may show rouleaux. Phosphate, ALP, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and PTHrP help if myeloma is excluded, followed by a search for solid tumours with CT. Calcium, renal function and the ECG are monitored.

Management starts with IV 0.9% sodium chloride to correct volume depletion and promote calcium excretion, with careful fluid balance given her renal impairment. Once rehydrated, an IV bisphosphonate inhibits osteoclast resorption, taking two to four days for full effect and adjusted for renal function; denosumab is an alternative in significant renal impairment. Drugs that raise calcium, such as thiazides and calcium or vitamin D supplements, are stopped. Glucocorticoids are useful when hypercalcaemia is due to myeloma or excess calcitriol. Urgent haematology referral is needed for definitive treatment of myeloma, which also addresses renal injury from light chains.

questions.q: Amira, 24, has had periods only four times a year since menarche, with increasing facial hair and acne. BMI is 31 kg/m² and she has acanthosis nigricans in the axillae. She is not on hormonal contraception and has no galactorrhoea. Pregnancy test is negative. (a) What is the most likely diagnosis and how is it made? (b) Which investigations exclude other causes? (c) Outline management, including if she wishes to conceive.
markScheme: Most likely polycystic ovary syndrome
Rotterdam criteria (2 of 3): oligo-/anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound or raised AMH in adults
Here oligomenorrhoea and clinical hyperandrogenism already satisfy two criteria
Exclude: pregnancy, thyroid dysfunction (TSH), hyperprolactinaemia (prolactin), non-classical CAH (17-hydroxyprogesterone)
Very high testosterone or rapid virilisation prompts search for androgen-secreting tumour; consider Cushing's if suggestive
Metabolic screening: HbA1c or OGTT, lipids, blood pressure; screen mood and sleep apnoea
Lifestyle and weight management as first step
Combined oral contraceptive for cycle control and hyperandrogenism, protecting endometrium; topical treatment or anti-androgen with contraception for hirsutism
Endometrial protection: risk of hyperplasia with prolonged amenorrhoea
Fertility: letrozole first line for ovulation induction; metformin may be added; gonadotrophins, laparoscopic ovarian drilling or IVF later
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The most likely diagnosis is polycystic ovary syndrome. It is diagnosed with the Rotterdam criteria, adopted by the 2023 international guideline: two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (or raised AMH in adults), once other causes are excluded. Amira's oligomenorrhoea and hirsutism with acne already satisfy two criteria, so ultrasound is not essential.

(b) Pregnancy has been excluded. TSH excludes thyroid dysfunction, prolactin excludes hyperprolactinaemia, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone excludes non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Total testosterone, or free androgen index, confirms biochemical hyperandrogenism; a markedly high level or rapid virilisation should prompt imaging for an androgen-secreting ovarian or adrenal tumour. Cushing's syndrome is considered if there are suggestive features. Because PCOS is linked to insulin resistance, she should have HbA1c or an oral glucose tolerance test, lipids and blood pressure checked, and be asked about mood and sleep.

(c) Lifestyle change and weight management are the foundation, since modest weight loss can restore ovulation and improve metabolic risk. If she does not wish to conceive, a combined oral contraceptive regulates bleeding, protects the endometrium from hyperplasia caused by unopposed oestrogen, and lowers free androgens by raising SHBG and suppressing LH. Hirsutism may also respond to cosmetic hair removal or an anti-androgen used with reliable contraception. Metformin can help metabolic features.

If she wishes to conceive, she should optimise weight, start folic acid and stop smoking. Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor that increases FSH by reducing oestrogen feedback, is first-line ovulation induction; metformin may be added. Second-line options include gonadotrophins with monitoring for ovarian hyperstimulation, laparoscopic ovarian drilling, and IVF.

questions.q: Mr Clarke, 34, has low libido, erectile dysfunction and reduced shaving frequency. He and his partner have tried to conceive for 18 months. He trains at a gym and admits past use of injected anabolic steroids, stopped four months ago. Morning testosterone is low on two occasions with LH and FSH low. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Discuss the differential diagnosis, investigation and management, explaining the physiology behind each step.
markScheme: Low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH indicates secondary (hypogonadotrophic) hypogonadism
Most likely cause: anabolic steroid-induced suppression of the HPG axis through negative feedback
Other secondary causes: pituitary tumour, hyperprolactinaemia, opioids, glucocorticoids, obesity, systemic illness, haemochromatosis, Kallmann syndrome
Azoospermia explained by low FSH and low intratesticular testosterone despite previous high serum androgen levels

Investigations: prolactin, other pituitary function (cortisol, thyroid), ferritin/transferrin saturation, pituitary MRI if indicated (e.g. very low testosterone, high prolactin, visual or other pituitary symptoms)
Examination: testicular volume, gynaecomastia, visual fields, BMI
Confirm with repeat semen analysis; recovery after steroid cessation can take many months
Exogenous testosterone would worsen fertility and must be avoided while he wishes to conceive
Fertility-preserving treatment: gonadotrophin therapy (hCG with or without FSH) to stimulate Leydig and Sertoli cells; SERMs used off-label in some cases
Advise against further steroid use, counsel about cardiovascular, hepatic and psychological effects; involve partner, fertility specialist
Assisted reproduction if spermatogenesis fails to recover
questions.modelAnswer:
Low testosterone with low LH and FSH defines secondary, or hypogonadotrophic, hypogonadism: the testes are not being stimulated. In a man who recently used anabolic steroids, the most likely cause is persistent suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Supraphysiological androgens and their aromatisation to oestradiol suppress GnRH, LH and FSH by negative feedback. While he was injecting, serum androgens were high, but intratesticular testosterone, which depends on LH-driven Leydig cell production and must be far higher than serum levels to support spermatogenesis, fell. With low FSH as well, Sertoli cells could not sustain sperm production, explaining azoospermia. After stopping, the axis can take many months to recover, leaving a period of symptomatic hypogonadism.

The differential still includes a pituitary adenoma, hyperprolactinaemia, opioid or glucocorticoid use, obesity, haemochromatosis, serious systemic illness and congenital causes such as Kallmann syndrome, although normal puberty argues against the latter. Examination should assess testicular volume, gynaecomastia, visual fields and BMI. Prolactin, thyroid function, morning cortisol and iron studies are checked. Pituitary MRI is indicated if testosterone is very low, prolactin is raised, other pituitary hormones are deficient or there are mass symptoms. Semen analysis is repeated to confirm azoospermia, and genetic testing considered if recovery fails.

Management must protect his fertility goals. Testosterone replacement would relieve symptoms but would further suppress LH and FSH and spermatogenesis, so it is inappropriate while he wishes to conceive. If the axis does not recover with time, fertility specialists may use gonadotrophin therapy: hCG acts like LH to restore intratesticular testosterone, with FSH added if needed. Selective oestrogen receptor modulators are sometimes used off-label to raise endogenous gonadotrophins. He should be counselled against further steroid use, including its cardiovascular, hepatic, psychiatric and fertility risks. His partner should be assessed in parallel, and surgical sperm retrieval with assisted reproduction is an option if spermatogenesis does not return.

questions.q: Mrs Adeyemi, 36, is 33 weeks into her first pregnancy. She has a severe frontal headache, visual flashing and epigastric pain. BP 164/112 mmHg on repeat; urine protein:creatinine ratio 85 mg/mmol; platelets 88 × 10⁹/L; ALT 210 U/L. Booking BP was 118/74 mmHg. (a) What is the diagnosis? (b) Explain the pathophysiology. (c) Outline management, including prevention in future pregnancies.
markScheme: Diagnosis: pre-eclampsia with severe features, likely HELLP syndrome (low platelets, raised liver enzymes; check haemolysis)
New hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria (uPCR above 30 mg/mmol) and organ dysfunction
Severe hypertension: 160/110 mmHg or more
Pathophysiology: abnormal trophoblast invasion and failed spiral artery remodelling causes placental ischaemia
Placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors (sFlt-1, soluble endoglin) with reduced PlGF, causing widespread endothelial dysfunction
Consequences: hypertension, glomerular endotheliosis and proteinuria, liver injury, thrombocytopenia, cerebral oedema and seizures
Immediate: admit to obstetric high-dependency care; urgent antihypertensive therapy (e.g. labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine classes)
Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease; monitor reflexes, respiration and urine output
Careful fluid restriction to avoid pulmonary oedema; fetal monitoring; antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity
Plan delivery after stabilisation, as delivery is definitive
Postpartum monitoring; long-term risk of cardiovascular disease and hypertension; aspirin from 12 weeks in future pregnancy
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Mrs Adeyemi has new hypertension after 20 weeks, significant proteinuria, and features of severe disease: severe hypertension (160/110 mmHg or more), headache and visual disturbance, epigastric pain, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases. This is pre-eclampsia with severe features, and the low platelets and raised ALT suggest HELLP syndrome; a blood film and LDH would look for haemolysis.

(b) In normal pregnancy, trophoblast invades the maternal spiral arteries and converts them into wide, low-resistance vessels. In pre-eclampsia this remodelling is incomplete, so placental perfusion is poor. The stressed placenta releases anti-angiogenic factors, notably soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) and soluble endoglin, which bind VEGF and placental growth factor. The resulting imbalance causes widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction: vasoconstriction and hypertension, glomerular endotheliosis with proteinuria, hepatic ischaemia, platelet consumption and cerebral vasogenic oedema leading to headache, visual symptoms and seizures. Low PlGF is the basis of PlGF-based testing.

(c) She needs admission to obstetric high-dependency care with senior obstetric, anaesthetic and midwifery input. Severe hypertension is treated urgently with antihypertensives such as labetalol, nifedipine or intravenous hydralazine to reduce stroke risk. Magnesium sulfate is given to prevent eclamptic seizures, with monitoring of reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output for toxicity. Fluids are restricted because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. The fetus is monitored with CTG and ultrasound, and antenatal corticosteroids are given to improve fetal lung maturity at 33 weeks. Delivery is the definitive treatment and is planned once she is stabilised; HELLP and severe features favour delivery rather than prolonged expectant care.

After delivery, BP and blood results are monitored because deterioration can occur postpartum. She should be counselled that recurrence is possible, and offered aspirin from 12 weeks in future pregnancies. Pre-eclampsia increases her lifelong risk of hypertension and cardiovascular disease, so long-term follow-up is advised.
